This post is a basic introduction to Reprap printers.

There are a number of printers you can buy that are all ready assembled and good to go. If you have more money than free time, it is probably best to go with an off the shelf model. If you like tinkering with things, and customizing things, Reprap is probably for you.

Reprap was originally based around the idea that 1 printer could print more printers.

In practice, 1 printer can print more plastic parts for other printers, but you will still need to buy all the rest, like power supply, wires, extruder, frame etc etc etc. Honestly what you will end up doing is using 1 printer to print improved parts for that 1 printer.

The thing about Reprap is, you can customize it to do almost anything. Paste Extruders (think printable chocolate), Laser Cutting / Engraving, CNC Routing and more are all possible with a Reprap. The same machine can even do all those things by swapping parts in and out. Off the shelf printers will severely limit your ability to customize these things.

So if you're still interested in Reprap you should probably be familiar with a few things:

IRC Chat

you are going to want some help at some point. The Reprap IRC channel is super helpful.

Ebay Patience

you are going to need some random parts. Sometimes they might come from China and take a month to get to you.

Soldering, Voltmeters, and Digital Calipers

with soldering, honestly, you dont have to be great, but if you can't solder at all, you're gonna have a bad time. Getting power to your printer will almost always require some sort of wire work. A decent voltmeter is going to come in handy once the thing is all the way built.

the Digital Calipers are really really important. Don't just try and use a tape measure. At times you will need like, millimeter precision. Using a digital calipers makes that realistic and takes 2 seconds to measure. The tool costs like $10 on ebay. Dont cheap out.

Arduino Experience

if you have at least done the "Blink" activity with an Arduino UNO you are prolly good to go. If you have never used an Arduino or wrote code near the metal (I love halt and catch fire) then things might get rough later on.

Startup Pro Tip

an easy way to get started and deal with the last two (and most important) issues is to order an Arduino MEGA first, but don't get just the board, get a starter kit. It will typically have some LEDs and other lil things you can use to get acquainted with most of the stuff you'll be doing later.

Choose Your Own Adventure

The next step would be to pick out what kind of printer you want to build. There are a number of options, but for your first printer there are a few recommended starting points. Personally I recommend the Prusa i3 or any of its variants. There a bunch of improvements and mods you can do to that model once its built and its very widely used, so lots of youtube videos and ebay parts.

The other popular model is the mendel series. The Mendel90 or MendelMax are two great options, but will probably cost more than an i3.

The Sky is the Limit

once you go down the rabbit hole of ordering parts and slowly building your printer there will be many lil issues and things to figure out, but if you pick a common enough design it will only be a quick trip to google or the IRC chat. Hopefully you have found this post helpful!

The fourth part of this poem feels like Eliot is trying to find an answer for everything, something that will make everything else make sense. It's a common underlying theme in most of his work, which he often highlights "trivial" moments - like

In the room the women go

Talking of Michelangelo

Which was a stand-alone verse in his Love Song, which focuses on the experience of aging, sorrow, and fear.

We all know that there are very few, if any, such effectual answers in this life, and would be even more rare in a surrealist dystopia. We cannot help but react in nonsensical ways to nonsensical circumstances (think: gaslighting, severe tragedies).

Also, Eliot’s footnote says that he’s referring to one of the Sanskrit holy texts, the Upanishads. If you look up the particular Upanishad he cites, you find the Babel theme: gods, men and demons all called on the Lord (at the same time) to speak to them, and when he replied "Da," but each group naturally interpreted this cryptic remark in a different way. So even if there is an answer, our human folly will probably pervert it, and when we no longer understand the answer, we see the world as nonsensical.

Do we even know if there's an answer? What if nothing means anything? What's a rational response to this uncertainty?

There really isn't one. So, Eliot reverts to childlike thinking, to anger, to loneliness, to absurdity.
